+43/44 if console moves to USB-CDC) + 3 free EXIO 34 / ~20 Wi-Fi CYW43439 802.11n 2.4 GHz RM2 (same chip) none 802.11n 2.4 GHz on-chip 802.11n 2.4 GHz Bluetooth 5.2 Classic + BLE (BTstack); A2DP source SBC/SBC-XQ only, CPU encode same none BLE 5.0 only — no Classic, no A2DP 4.2 Classic + BLE; A2DP source SBC in ESP-IDF SD interface PIO SDIO 4-bit (15.6 MHz bench, ~25 MHz max) PIO SDIO TF slot, SDIO 4-bit via PIO TF slot on hardware SDMMC up to 40 MHz (CLK GPIO4, CMD 5, D0 6, D3/CS 2; D1/D2 to verify) hardware SDMMC Display on board — — 2.41" AMOLED 450×600 RM690B0, QSPI 4-lane (CS 9, CLK 10, SIO 11–14, RST 15, TE 16, PWR_EN 17), FT6336 touch (I²C 6/7, INT 4, RST 5) same panel (CS 9, CLK 10, D0–3 11–14, RST 21; TE/EN/TP_INT on EXIO0–2; I²C 47/48) — Power / battery VSYS diode, no charger LDO, no charger ETA6098 1 A charger, 2-pin MX1.25 battery, BAT ADC, power key ETA6098 charger, battery connector, BAT ADC GPIO17, key GPIO15, BAT_Control GPIO16 — Extras — — PCF85063 RTC, QMI8658 IMU, buttons PCF85063 RTC, QMI8658 IMU, TCA9554-class IO expander (EXIO), buttons — USB micro-B USB-C USB-C USB-C — Debug access SWD 3-pin JST-SH (Debug Probe) SWD pads/header (check board) no SWD header — SWCLK/SWD go only to the chip; debug via USB (picotool/UF2) + UART0 on GPIO0/1 built-in USB-JTAG over the USB-C (OpenOCD, no probe) UART bootloader; JTAG on GPIO12–15 Deep sleep ~0.2 mA (radio off) same same ~10 µA ~10 µA Licensing BTstack/cyw43 grant covers Pico W / RM2 grant covers RM2 n/a ESP-IDF Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0

Consequences. (1) The 477/520 KB RAM squeeze disappears on any PSRAM board; RP2350 PSRAM is memory-mapped through the XIP cache (~4× slower than SRAM), fine for audio rings, LVGL buffers and artwork. The Plus-W needs an APS6404L fitted (WSON-8 C3040877 is the stocked variant). (2) Bluetooth is the fork: RP2350 + CYW43439/RM2 gives Classic BT with SBC only; ESP32-S3 has no Classic BT, so the S3 AMOLED board cannot drive the AirPods without a QCC module; only the original ESP32 has Classic + A2DP source in a permissive stack. (3) ESP32-S3 and ESP32 have hardware SDMMC; RP2350 SD is PIO and clock-limited. (4) The RP2350 AMOLED board is the nearest thing to the final board (RP2350B + PSRAM + charger + RTC + SDIO slot + panel) minus a radio and minus SWD — it is the right place to develop the AMOLED driver and power path, with the Pico 2 W kept for anything that needs the Debug Probe. Testbed stays on the Pico 2 W until the AMOLED boards arrive.

docs.title: Click feedback — Taptic-class actuators (5 Nov 2026)
docs.text:
A "Taptic Engine" is a large, well-damped X-axis LRA driven with short waveforms, first-half-cycle overdrive and active braking. The DRV2605L already on the bench does all three in LRA closed-loop mode; the ERM was buzzy because an ERM cannot brake. Candidates for the A/B against the stock piezo buzzer:

Option Size Drive Feel / notes Salvaged iPhone 7/8/SE2 Taptic Engine ~35 × 11 × 4.5 mm DRV2605L LRA mode (auto-cal finds the params) or DRV2624/2625 The real thing; thick shell only; reference sample Off-the-shelf X-axis rectangular LRA (Vybronics VLV101040A class) ~10 × 10 × 4 to 20 × 10 × 3.5 mm DRV2605L LRA mode 80 % of the Taptic feel, datasheeted, £1–3; best fit for the thin shell Piezo haptic: TDK PowerHap 0904H014 + Boreas BOS1901 9 × 4 × 1.4 mm; BOS1901 boosts 3.3 V to ±95 V internally BOS1901 (I²C + waveform in; senses presses) Sharpest, fastest (<1 ms), thinnest, lowest power; "tick" rather than "thud" — ideal for a wheel detent Coin LRA (VG1040003D) 10 × 3.6 mm DRV2605L Softer, slightly ringy — fallback

Decision after the A/B; the final board keeps a piezo-buzzer footprint plus whichever haptic wins.

docs.title: Display bring-up tests
docs.text: An interactive test menu for the Phase 1 display (Adafruit 2.0" 320x240 IPS TFT, ST7789, SPI1). The menu runs on the Pico and is driven from the PC's serial console: you type the keys on the PC, not on the Pico.

docs.title: Confirmed hardware settings
docs.text:
Confirmed on the bench (2026-11-02):

Setting Value Orientation / colour order MADCTL 0x60 (MX + MV, landscape), RGB order Inversion INVON (the panel needs it) Backlight GP8 PWM, active high System clock clk_sys = clk_peri = 125 MHz SPI1 62.5 MHz exactly (clk_peri / 2), 16-bit frames, DMA Console UART0 GP0/GP1, 115200 8N1 Column/row offset 0 / 0 (test 3 border visible on all four edges)

Measured on the bench (2026-11-02), all eight tests passing visual checks:

Measurement Result Full-screen blit from flash (test 5) 22 ms Same image via strip renderer (test 5) 23 ms Strip-rendered animation (test 7) 46.05 fps, 7.07 MB/s — 90 % of the 7.81 MB/s / 50.8 fps ceiling Random shapes (test 4) 91 strip-rendered frames in 2012 ms

docs.title: Build, flash, run
docs.text:
export PICO_SDK_PATH=$HOME/pico/pico-sdk
scripts/build.sh rp2350
scripts/flash.sh rp2350 display_test
scripts/console.sh          # minicom on the Debug Probe UART; type the keys here

Reset the board with the console already open to see the start-up line that reports clk_sys, clk_peri and the real SPI baud rate. On the PC, scripts/build.sh host builds the same menu as build/host/hal/host/display_test (keys from the terminal; with SDL installed it shows a window, otherwise set NEUPOD_DISPLAY_PPM=out.ppm to capture each frame). The Now Playing screen alone: build/host/hal/host/now_playing [8|16] [light].

docs.title: Menu keys
docs.text:
Key Action 1-8 Run that test a Run all, about 3 s each q Stop the running test and return to the menu b Toggle BGR order (MADCTL bit 3) i Toggle inversion r Cycle rotation: MADCTL 0x60, 0xA0, 0xE0, 0x20 m Print MADCTL and inversion state p Corner pattern: red top-left, green top-right, blue bottom-left, white bottom-right h / Enter Reprint the menu

b, i and r also work while a test is showing a static screen. Each test prints a VISUAL CHECK: line describing what you should see; if a display call fails it prints FAIL instead of relying on your eyes.

docs.title: Tests and what to look for
docs.text: # Test Should look like 1 Backlight White screen fades dark, full, dark over 4 s with no flicker or steps, then holds at 10 %, 50 %, 100 % 2 Colours Red, green, blue, white, black fills, uniform; 8 bars white-yellow-cyan-green-magenta-red-blue-black; four 256-step gradients. RGB565 has only 32/64/32 levels, so visible steps are expected 3 Sharpness 1-px checkerboard and gratings crisp; 1-px white border with all four edges visible; centred crosshair 4 Geometry Random lines, rectangles and circles (round, not oval), then a 32 x 24 grid of square cells 5 Image Same picture twice (one DMA from flash, then strip-rendered): arrow points right, yellow mark top-left, magenta top-right 6 Text Both fonts legible; Now Playing screen white-on-black then black-on-white in both fonts 7 Animation Bouncing ball with fading trail; prints fps and SPI MB/s against the 7.81 MB/s ceiling at 62.5 MHz 8 Sleep Image goes blank for 2 s, then returns without being redrawn

docs.title: Failure checklist
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause / action Image mirrored or rotated (test 5 arrow not pointing right, corner pattern in wrong corners) Wrong MADCTL orientation bits. Press r; confirmed value is 0x60 Red and blue swapped (red fill looks blue; yellow mark looks cyan) BGR bit. Press b Negative colours (white fill is black, red looks cyan) Inversion. Press i; the panel needs inversion on Smearing, noise, random pixels or grey haze on the 1-px gratings (test 3) SPI too fast for the wiring: shorten wires, add ground, or lower the SPI rate Garbage or horizontally shifted image, commands appearing as pixels D/C or CS timing: check GP16 (D/C) and GP13 (CS) wiring and that nothing else drives them Border line missing on one edge, or wrapped to the opposite side Column/row offset (TFT_COL_OFFSET / TFT_ROW_OFFSET) Backlight brightest at 0 and dark at 255 Backlight polarity inverted (it is active high on this board) Backlight never changes GP8 wiring, or PWM not attached to the backlight pin Blank or white after wake (test 8) Sleep/wake timing; the ST7789 should keep its frame memory in sleep Test 7 well below ~46 fps (measured) / 50.8 fps raw ceiling Clock not 125 MHz or SPI below 62.5 MHz: check the start-up line

docs.title: Source layout
docs.text: The tests live in app/tests/display_tests.c and use the portable drawing layer in app/gfx/ (primitives, two bitmap fonts, a strip renderer that draws 320x16 strips into two 10 KB buffers while DMA sends the previous one). Fonts: app/gfx/fonts/README.md. Images: tools/README.md. Pixels are native-endian RGB565 everywhere, matching the driver's 16-bit SPI frames.

docs.title: ESP32-S3 platform (Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-2.41)
docs.text:
The full neuPod runtime on an ESP32-S3 dev board: boot self-checks, settings, storage and library, the LVGL UI, input, and the audio core with a null sink (the board has no audio hardware). It is built from the same app/ sources as the RP2350 neupod target, with a board HAL in platforms/esp32s3/main/hal/. This is a dev platform, not a product target (the product target is the RP2350B, ADR-0001); it exists to run the real runtime on a touch AMOLED panel and to prove the HAL interfaces on a third architecture.

Not in yet: Wi-Fi and BLE (the radio HAL answers "not present" and nothing joins a network), a battery gauge (the board has no fuel gauge; the battery divider on GPIO17 is not read), the IMU and RTC.

Chip ESP32-S3R8: dual Xtensa LX7 at 240 MHz, 8 MB octal PSRAM, 16 MB flash. Wi-Fi + BLE 5 only: no Classic Bluetooth, so no A2DP Display 450 x 600 RM690B0 AMOLED on QSPI (SPI2: CS 9, CLK 10, D0-3 11-14, RST 21), used as 600 x 450 landscape (MADCTL 0x30). Panel power enable and TE are on the TCA9554 expander (EXIO1, EXIO0); board.c must write it (output 0x03, config 0xDC) every boot or the panel stays dark Touch FT6336 at I2C 0x38, reset GPIO3, polled (its interrupt is EXIO2) I2C one bus, SDA 47 / SCL 48: TCA9554 0x20, FT6336 0x38, QMI8658 0x6B, PCF85063 0x51 microSD SPI (SPI3): CS 2, SCK 4, MOSI 5, MISO 6, 20 MHz Power KEY_BAT GPIO15 (side key, active low), BAT_CTRL GPIO16 (soft latch: driven high first thing, or the board switches off on battery when the key is released), BAT_ADC GPIO17 Console the USB-C port, native USB-Serial/JTAG (303a:1001), stdio plus the key map of Runtime

The pin map and the panel facts were proven by the bring-up probe (testbed/esp32amoled241/bringup).

docs.title: Build and flash
docs.text:
Same container as CI (ESP-IDF v5.3.2). From the repository root, with the submodules fetched (git submodule update --init lib/lvgl):

docker run --rm --user $(id -u):$(id -g) -e HOME=/tmp -v "$PWD":/project -w /project espressif/idf:v5.3.2 \
  bash -c '. $IDF_PATH/export.sh && scripts/build.sh esp32s3'

or, with ESP-IDF installed, . ~/esp/esp-idf/export.sh && scripts/build.sh esp32s3. The result is build/esp32s3/neupod.bin (about 1 MB of a 4 MB app partition). Flash the bootloader, partition table and app (this replaces whatever is on the board; the factory image is restored with esptool write-flash 0 factory-flash-16MB.bin from a backup taken first):

cd build/esp32s3
esptool --chip esp32s3 --port /dev/serial/by-id/usb-Espressif_USB_JTAG_serial_debug_unit_* -b 460800 write-flash @flash_args

The console is the same USB port (115200 is nominal; it is USB). Keys typed there drive the UI like the Pico rig's UART.

docs.title: How it differs from the other platforms
docs.text:
FatFs. ESP-IDF ships its own fatfs component (ff.h, diskio.h, f_* and disk_* symbols), which collides with neuPod's. The build excludes the IDF component entirely (EXCLUDE_COMPONENTS fatfs in platforms/esp32s3/CMakeLists.txt) and uses app/third_party/fatfs with the shared ffconf.h and app/storage/diskio.c over hal_storage, the same layering as the Y2 and the host. hal_storage talks to the card through IDF's sdspi host and sdmmc protocol code (identification, sector read and write). The reasons: the card's file system behaviour (exFAT, long names, the FF_* options the library and settings code were tested with) stays identical on every board, the vendored copy has one configuration check, and there is no ff.h on any include path to pick the wrong one. IDF's VFS/esp_vfs_fat layer is not used: nfs.h is the file API.

RTOS. app/os/os_freertos.c builds unchanged apart from three guarded items: the FreeRTOS headers live under freertos/; every runtime task is created with xTaskCreatePinnedToCore(..., core 0); and os_start() retires app_main's task (the IDF scheduler is already running). Stacks are doubled (OS_STACK_SCALE 2): Xtensa's windowed-register frames and newlib's printf are larger than Thumb-2's, and the library scan overflowed the 8 KB storage stack on the bench (the hardware stack-end watchpoint, CONFIG_FREERTOS_WATCHPOINT_END_OF_STACK, is on to catch the next one).

The audio core (ADR-0011). The RP2350's core 1 is bare metal; the S3's FreeRTOS is SMP, so the shape is kept with tasks:

Where What CPU 0 every RTOS task of the runtime (storage, UI, input, monitor, check tasks, haptic, wifi) and all IDF service tasks CPU 1 audio: the audio core loop (audio_core_main, priority 5, 28 KB stack), and vclk: the block clock task (priority 20)

hal_audio.c is the null sink with a real-time block clock: a 1 MHz general-purpose timer interrupt on CPU 1 (allocated by the core that calls hal_audio_open(), deadlines absolute and drift-free) wakes vclk, which calls the block callback. The callback was written for interrupt context, so a task that preempts the decoder on the same CPU is a safe home for it. Measured: 5804 us period, jitter under 70 us, 0 under-runs. The core-1 rules scripts (check_core1_rules, the closure check) apply to the RP2350 image only.

Memory. 512 KB internal SRAM is shared by the static data, task stacks and DMA buffers; the 8 MB PSRAM takes the big buffers. By object file, in main/linker.lf (no attributes in app/):

In PSRAM Why there codec arena (99 KB), compressed-data ring (32 KB) decoder working memory and the SD-to-decoder ring; not latency critical UI render buffers (72 KB at 600x450) too big for internal RAM next to the stacks LVGL's pool (192 KB, NEUPOD_LVGL_POOL_BYTES) widgets, styles, layers; sized like the hosted builds: 72 KB ran out on the Music screens display shadow (527 KB, allocated at run time) see below

Internal: the PCM ring (32 KB), the library buffers, a 2 KB SD staging buffer (PSRAM or unaligned buffers are copied through it, so no read or write depends on a bounce-buffer allocation), the display's two DMA strips (19 KB each), task stacks. After boot about 76 KB of internal heap is free (32 KB at the lowest, while the boot-check tasks run together): enough now, but the Wi-Fi/BLE stacks will need to be budgeted against it (trim the doubled stacks that measure small: the monitor line prints each task's stack-free minimum).

Display bring-up (what the dark-panel hunt found). The bring-up probe and the first runtime builds left the panel dark, while the factory image lit it. The factory firmware's init table was read out of its image (and matches Waveshare's 10_FactoryProgram demo source). It differs from the probe's in the tail: after sleep-out it sets the window, sends display-on (0x29), MADCTL 0x30 and full brightness (0x51 0xFF) inside the init, before any pixel, and the driver sends 0x29 once more; the probe switched the display on only after the first frame. The expander turned out to be the real cause (bench, 21 Nov 2026): at a cold power-on the TCA9554 reads input 0xFE, output 0xFF, polarity 0x00, config 0xFF (all inputs) and the panel stays dark; after the factory firmware has run it reads output 0x03, config 0xDC (EXIO0 and EXIO1 PWR_EN driven high, EXIO5 driven low, the rest inputs) and the panel lights. That state survives an ESP32 reset and is lost only on a power cycle, so the earlier "fix" (the factory init table) only seemed to work on a warm expander. board.c now writes output 0x03 then config 0xDC and waits 20 ms before display init; this lit the panel from a full cold power cycle. Display tests must start from a full power cycle (USB and battery both out). Note the schematic labels EXIO0 "TE", which would be an input from the panel, yet the factory drives it high as an output, and so do we because that is the state proven to work; what EXIO0 and EXIO5 really do is not known. hal_display.c follows the factory sequence. The probe's esp_lcd_sh8601 2.0.1 is the same driver version the factory uses, with the same QSPI configuration (40 MHz, mode 0, 0x02/0x32 framing).

Display. hal_display.c talks to the RM690B0 through esp_lcd's SPI panel IO in QSPI mode (SH8601 framing: opcode 0x02 for commands, 0x32 + 0x2C00 for pixels), so no extra component is needed (the probe used espressif/esp_lcd_sh8601; the runtime does not). The controller wants windows that start even and end odd, and LVGL hands over arbitrary partial areas: a full shadow of the panel in PSRAM, already in the panel's byte order, takes each hal_display_blit() and the area is pushed from it widened to even edges, whatever the caller's alignment. Landscape is MADCTL 0x30 and a 16-row offset. hal_display_name() is RM690B0; brightness is command 0x51.

Input. One side key (hal_input_power_key(), GPIO15, active low) and the touch panel (hal_touch.h). There is no wheel and no Hold switch: hal_input_init() answers HAL_ENODEV, so the boot check marks the wheel degraded, exactly as on the RP2350 AMOLED board (touch and the console keys do not depend on it). A key press that is already down at power-on is ignored until it has been released once. The runtime's input task owns the touch controller: it calls hal_touch_init() under the I2C mutex once the bus is up and polls hal_touch_read() every 2 ms (app/input/touch_gesture.c, Touch); hal_touch.c throttles the bus to one read per 8 ms and uses the i2c_master driver, which locks the bus per transaction, so it shares the bus safely with hal_i2c. The touch HAL maps the controller's portrait coordinates to landscape (x = y, y = 449 - x; the factory demo's x = 599 - y, y = x came out 180 degrees rotated on the bench, 2026-11-15). The display (factory init table) and this mapping are bench-confirmed; the three TOUCH_* switches at the top of hal_touch.c are the one place to change the mapping.

Radio. hal_wifi_present() is false, every Wi-Fi call answers HAL_ENODEV, and hal_bt_init() answers HAL_ENOTSUP; the boot check reports both as unavailable. No network is ever joined. hal_system_late_init() has nothing to start.

Crypto. app/crypto is compiled against IDF's mbed TLS (hardware AES/SHA); hal_chip_id() is the factory MAC. hal_random() is the hardware RNG register, which without the radio on is a noise source rather than a certified TRNG: fine for the secrets file's per-record nonces, to be revisited when Wi-Fi/BLE are.

Power. BAT_CTRL is latched high by the first start-up init function of the image (ESP_SYSTEM_INIT_FN in board.c, before the heap and PSRAM are up), and the 0.3 s PSRAM memory test is off, to keep the window in which a power-on key press could be released early as short as possible. hal_system_poweroff() drops the latch, waits 200 ms and returns false if the board is still running (USB power: the charger keeps it alive; it is probed, not assumed), so the UI takes its "powering off" overlay away; on battery the power simply goes. hal_random() is the hardware RNG register (not a certified TRNG while the radio is off; fine for per-record nonces; revisit with Wi-Fi/BLE).

docs.title: UI profile
docs.text:
The build sets NEUPOD_UI_PROFILE=600x450 (default for this platform, platforms/esp32s3/CMakeLists.txt; -DNEUPOD_UI_PROFILE=320x240 gives the small one, which then sits in the top-left corner). The profile is a compile-time constant, wired through the IDF component as NEUPOD_UI_PROFILE_600. Its two partial-render buffers (600 x 30 x 2 bytes each, 72 KB together) are placed in PSRAM with the other big buffers (ui in linker.lf): they would not fit the internal RAM next to the stacks. Bench, 600x450: boot frame 7.5 ms average, a full-pane Settings screen about 40 ms average (the pane is redrawn whole), internal heap free 76 KB after boot (32 KB at the lowest).

Measured stack minimums (bench, idle UI): audio 27.2 KB free of 28 KB, vclk 4.3 KB of 5 KB, input 1.8 KB of 4 KB, storage 9.4 KB of 16 KB, ui 16.5 KB of 24 KB. A decode on the audio core has not been measured (there is no music on the bench card yet): the audio stack is 28 KB and vclk 5 KB so that the deeper decoder path has room; re-check core1_stack_free in the monitor line the first time a FLAC and an MP3 play.

docs.title: Bench result (14 Nov 2026, 600x450 profile)
docs.text:
Boot log, USB console, on the board with a 32 GB FAT32 card (no music on it):

neuPod 0.1.0-dev (nogit) starting on esp32s3
display: RM690B0 600x450 landscape, QSPI 40 MHz, shadow 527 KB in PSRAM
boot: display   ok      : RM690B0 600x450
boot: battery   DEGRADED: gauge (0x36): no response
boot: haptics   DEGRADED: driver (0x5A): no response
boot: audio     DEGRADED: output is the null sink (no DAC output)
boot: wifi      DEGRADED: no Wi-Fi on this platform (Bluetooth only)
boot: storage   ok      : SDHC 31.2 GB, FAT32, read-only
boot: bluetooth DEGRADED: Bluetooth start failed: not supported
boot: wheel     DEGRADED: receiver: no response
touch: FT6336 chip id 0x64 (0x64 = FT6336) firmware 0x01 vendor 0x11
input: touch panel ready (600x450)

The UI navigates from the console keys (Home, Music, Extras, Settings), the library scan runs and finishes, and a changed setting is written to the card and read back after a reset (settings: loaded (7 items, seq 3)), which proves the whole SD path: sdspi, sdmmc, diskio.c, FatFs and the write lock.

docs.title: I2C peripherals: fuel gauge and haptics
docs.text:
Phase 1 breadboard: one I2C bus, I2C0 on the Pico 2 W, SDA = GP20, SCL = GP21, 400 kHz (fall back to 100 kHz if NACKs appear). Both breakouts carry their own pull-ups, so the firmware keeps the RP2350 internal pull-ups off (the pad reset state is pull-down enabled, so they are switched off explicitly). See Phase 1 wiring.

Device Board Address HAL Driver MAX17048 fuel gauge Adafruit MAX17048 0x36 hal_battery.h app/drivers/max17048.c DRV2605L haptic driver Adafruit DRV2605L 0x5A hal_haptic.h app/drivers/drv2605l.c

hal_power.h is kept for sleep and power-state control only; its old battery snapshot was never implemented and is replaced by hal_battery.h.

docs.title: Bus layer (hal_i2c.h)
docs.text:
• Every call is bounded: timeout = 2 x the byte time at the actual baud, never below 2 ms.
  • A NACK is a normal answer and never causes recovery. Only a timeout, or a line that is still low 100 us after a failed transfer, starts recovery: reset the controller, then (if SDA/SCL is low) switch the pins to GPIO, clock up to 9 SCL pulses (drive low / release, never drive high), generate a STOP and restore the I2C function. hal_i2c_get_stats() counts errors and recoveries.
  • Probing uses a 1-byte read (a zero-length write is unreliable on the RP2040/RP2350 controller) and skips the reserved ranges 0x00-0x07 and 0x78-0x7F.
  • Arbitration loss cannot be detected on the RP2350: the SDK clears the abort-source register before the HAL can read it, so ARB_LOST is never reported there. A lost arbitration that leaves a line low shows up as a stuck bus.
  • Reserved addresses are refused (BAD_PARAM) by every call, not just probes.
  • Dropping from 400 to 100 kHz is never automatic: hal_i2c_set_baud() is called by the test (or application) deliberately.

docs.title: MAX17048 (0x36)
docs.text:
Registers are 16-bit big-endian. Used here:

Reg Name Scaling / use 0x02 VCELL 78.125 uV per LSB (mV = raw x 5 / 64, rounded) 0x04 SOC 1/256 % per LSB (high byte = whole percent) 0x06 MODE bit 14 = quick-start 0x08 VERSION reads 0x001X 0x0A HIBRT high byte hibernate threshold 0.208 %/h per LSB, low byte active threshold 1.25 mV per LSB 0x0C CONFIG high byte RCOMP; low byte SLEEP (b7), ALSC (b6), ALRT (b5), ATHD (b4:0): alert at 32 - ATHD % 0x16 CRATE signed, 0.208 %/h per LSB 0x1A STATUS RI b8, VH b9, VL b10, VR b11, HD b12, SC b13, ENVR b14 0xFE CMD 0x5400 = power-on reset (the chip may NACK the write as it resets)

hal_battery_init() also clears STATUS.RI (power-up/reset indicator) so a later RI means a fresh reset; hal_battery_reset() waits 250 ms after the reset command and leaves RI set. Quick-start is only valid with no load on the cell. HIBRT as read from the bench chip: 0x8030 (observed, not asserted by the tests).

The driver uses integers only: millivolts, SOC in 1/256 %, rate in milli-percent per hour. A cell below 2.5 V counts as "no battery".

Source check

The MAX17048 scaling above comes from the Maxim/Analog Devices register descriptions as recalled when writing the driver; the datasheet PDF could not be downloaded in the build environment, so it is not yet cross-checked line by line. Check VCELL against a multimeter on the cell during bench test 2.

Bench note: the gauge is powered from the battery side. With no LiPo, or with a flat one, 0x36 disappears from the bus (a flat LiPo made 0x36 vanish on the bench). That is expected, not a wiring fault.

docs.title: DRV2605L (0x5A)
docs.text:
Checked against TI datasheet SLOS854D. Used here:

Reg Name Use 0x00 STATUS b7:5 DEVICE_ID (7 = DRV2605L), b3 DIAG_RESULT (1 = calibration failed; clears on read) 0x01 MODE b7 reset, b6 standby, b2:0: 0 internal trigger, 5 RTP, 7 auto-calibration 0x02 RTP_INPUT real-time amplitude 0x03 LIBRARY 1-5 and 7 ERM libraries A-F, 6 LRA 0x04-0x0B WAVEFORM_SEQ effect id 1-123, or bit 7 set = wait (n x 10 ms); 0 ends the sequence 0x0C GO start (clears itself at the end of playback / calibration) 0x16 / 0x17 RATED_VOLTAGE / OD_CLAMP see below 0x18 / 0x19 A_CAL_COMP / A_CAL_BEMF calibration results 0x1A FEEDBACK_CONTROL b7 ERM(0)/LRA(1), b6:4 brake factor, b3:2 loop gain, b1:0 BEMF gain 0x1B-0x1E CONTROL1-4 drive time, sample/blanking/idiss, ERM open-loop and RTP format, auto-cal time

docs.title: Motor
docs.text:
Adafruit 1201 "Vibrating Mini Motor Disc": ERM, 10 mm coin, brushed, rated 3.0 V (operates 2-5 V), about 11,000 rpm, about 75-100 mA running. Default drive mode is ERM open loop with ROM library 2 (TS2200 library B); the voltage ceiling is 3.6 V. Build-time defaults: NEUPOD_HAPTIC_ACTUATOR=HAL_HAPTIC_ERM and NEUPOD_HAPTIC_ERM_LOOP=HAL_HAPTIC_LOOP_OPEN (or HAL_HAPTIC_LOOP_CLOSED). Test menu keys: o toggles open/closed loop, e / l select ERM / LRA.

Why open loop: on the bench the closed-loop auto-calibration did not converge on this motor (3.0 V rated, 3.3 V supply; DIAG_RESULT failed after 1844 ms) and the motor buzzed instead of clicking. By user decision the ERM now runs open loop, which is also how Adafruit's own library drives this motor. Closed loop stays available (o key or build flag) for later experiments. The LRA path (library 6, LRA bit) is selectable at run time (Settings > Haptics > Actuator) and described below.

docs.title: LRA: LEADER LD0832AA
docs.text:
Target actuator for the final board: 8 mm coin LRA, rated 2.0 V rms, resonance about 235 Hz (build defaults in HAL_HAPTIC_LRA_LD0832AA, hal_haptic_lra_params_t; override at run time with hal_haptic_set_lra_params()). Not confirmed from the LCSC datasheet (C2682305): the datasheet could not be fetched from the build host, so 2.0 V rms and 235 Hz are the figures from the brief. Everything below is computed from those two numbers, so a different actuator only needs different parameters. The peak ceiling (2.8 V, 2 V x sqrt(2) floored) is a design choice, not a datasheet figure.

Value Formula (datasheet SLOS854D) Result LIBRARY LRA library 6 FEEDBACK N_ERM_LRA = 1, brake factor 2, loop gain 2, BEMF gain 2 (calibration overwrites the gain) 0xAA RATED_VOLTAGE Eq. 5: V rms = 20.58 mV x RV / sqrt(1 - (4 x tSAMPLE + 300 us) x f), tSAMPLE = 300 us, so RV = floor(2000 x sqrt(1 - 1500 us x 235) / 20.58) 78 (0x4E) OD_CLAMP Eq. 9: V peak = 21.22 mV x OD, so OD = floor(2800 / 21.22) 131 (0x83) = 2.78 V CONTROL1 STARTUP_BOOST + DRIVE_TIME = (half period - 0.5 ms) / 0.1 ms; half period 2.128 ms 0x90 (2.1 ms) CONTROL2 SAMPLE_TIME 3, BLANKING 1, IDISS 1 (datasheet defaults) 0xF5 CONTROL3 ERM_OPEN_LOOP and LRA_OPEN_LOOP cleared (closed loop, auto-resonance), RTP signed 0x80 CONTROL4 AUTO_CAL_TIME = 3 0x30

Click effect on an LRA: library 6 effect 4, Sharp Click 100 % (ERM keeps effect 3).

docs.title: Calibration and persistence
docs.text:
hal_haptic_calibrate() follows datasheet 8.5.6: MODE = 7, write the inputs above, GO, poll GO every 10 ms (through the delay hook, drv2605l_set_delay_fn; the firmware installs the scheduler delay so other tasks run), read STATUS DIAG_RESULT (1 = failed), then A_CAL_COMP, A_CAL_BEMF and BEMF_GAIN. A failure or timeout rebuilds the chip from reset with the previous good values.

The haptic task (core 0) owns this. The results are stored in the settings store (NPhc, 9 bytes: version, actuator, comp, bemf, gain, rated mV, peak mV, resonance Hz; version 2, 11 bytes) and re-applied on every boot, so the motor spins for the calibration once per actuator. It runs automatically when an LRA is selected (or built in) and no matching record exists, once the settings are known (the card's values have loaded, or there is no working card; a boot without a card cannot store it, so it repeats each boot). If the record cannot be stored (store full) the row shows Failed and a console line says so, and on demand from Settings > Haptics > Calibrate. Changing the actuator type, or the rated voltage, peak voltage or resonance (OD_CLAMP is a calibration input), makes the stored record not match, so it recalibrates (as does an old version 1 record, which had no peak); switching back and forth between types re-runs it for each. The task holds the I2C bus (the gauge read waits) for about a second but sleeps between polls, never blocking the UI. Clicks during it: rt_haptic_click() drops the request while the state is RUNNING (nothing is queued), and the task drains its queue when a calibration starts and again when it ends, which also discards a click that raced past the check. If the automatic attempt fails it is not retried until the next boot or a manual Calibrate.

docs.title: Click setting and rate limit
docs.text: Settings > Click: Piezo / Haptic / Both / Off (NPck 2 / 1 / 3 / 0). There is no piezo driver yet (NEUPOD_PIEZO_FITTED is 0), so the menu cycles Haptic / Off only; a Piezo or Both value already stored is accepted but silent (rt_piezo_click() is a stub). Haptic clicks go through a 2-deep queue and a 35 ms gate (haptic_gate_pass): a fast wheel spin drops requests instead of queueing them.

docs.title: Bring-up order (motor safety)
docs.text: In open loop OD_CLAMP is the full-scale drive (21.59 mV x OD, datasheet Eq. 6), so the clamp value must always match the loop mode in effect: 182 (the closed-loop value) would be about 3.93 V in open loop. The chip powers up open-loop. The driver therefore leaves standby, sets the chosen loop bit in CONTROL3 and reads it back, writes the feedback/timing registers, and writes RATED_VOLTAGE then OD_CLAMP last. If any step fails the chip is put back into standby and play/click/RTP/calibrate return an error until init succeeds. A failed or timed-out calibration resets the chip and re-applies the previous good calibration. The test menu puts the driver in a safe state (RTP 0, GO 0, standby) as soon as the bus comes up, and back in standby after every haptic test. The l (LRA) key is disabled unless the test is built with NEUPOD_I2C_TEST_ALLOW_LRA.

docs.title: Register values: ERM open loop (default)
docs.text:
Value Formula (datasheet Eq. 6) Result CONTROL3 ERM_OPEN_LOOP = 1 (power-on default), RTP signed 0xA0 OD_CLAMP V = 21.59 mV x OD, so OD = floor(3600 / 21.59) 166 (0xA6) = 3.584 V (167 would be 3.605 V) RATED_VOLTAGE ignored in open loop (datasheet 8.5.2.1); the closed-loop value is written as a safe one 141 (0x8D)

The datasheet constant is 21.59 mV per step for ERM open loop (Eq. 6), not 21.96 mV; the maximum open-loop clamp is therefore 166, enforced by the tests. Open-loop RTP is signed: 0 = no drive, 127 = +OD_CLAMP, negative values drive in reverse (braking). The ramp test only uses 0 to 127 to 0.

docs.title: Register values: ERM closed loop (optional, datasheet default timings)
docs.text:
Timings used: DRIVE_TIME = 0x13 (ERM: 1 ms + 19 x 0.2 ms = 4.8 ms), BLANKING_TIME = 1 (75 us), IDISS_TIME = 1 (75 us); SAMPLE_TIME is LRA-only and left at 3. CONTROL1 = 0x93, CONTROL2 = 0xF5.

Value Formula (datasheet) Result RATED_VOLTAGE Eq. 4: V = 21.18 mV x RV, so RV = floor(3000 / 21.18) 141 (0x8D) = 2.986 V OD_CLAMP Eq. 8: V = 21.64 mV x OD x (4.8 ms - 300 us) / (4.8 ms + 75 us + 75 us), so OD = floor(3600 / 19.673 mV) 182 (0xB6) = 3.580 V (183 would give 3.6001 V, over the limit) FEEDBACK (pre-cal) ERM, brake factor 2, loop gain 2, BEMF gain 2 (power-on default; calibration overwrites it) 0x2A CONTROL3 ERM_OPEN_LOOP cleared (power-on default is open loop), RTP format signed 0x80 CONTROL4 AUTO_CAL_TIME = 3 (1000-1200 ms) 0x30

Brake factor 2, loop gain 2 and AUTO_CAL_TIME 3 are the "valid for most actuators" values in the datasheet calibration procedure. The floors are deliberate: the register never exceeds the requested voltage. The output cannot exceed the DRV2605L supply either (3.3 V on the breakout unless VIN is higher), so the real ceiling on this bench is the supply, not 3.6 V.

docs.title: Real-time playback
docs.text: Signed format (the power-on default). Closed loop (bidirectional): 0x00 = no drive, 0x7F (127) = full rated voltage, 0x3F about half; negative values act as zero. Open loop: 0x7F = +OD_CLAMP, 0x81 = -OD_CLAMP (reverse drive). The ramp test uses 0 to 127 to 0, which is safe in both.

docs.title: Click latency
docs.text: hal_haptic_click_prepare(effect) loads the sequencer once; hal_haptic_click() is then a single two-byte I2C write (GO). Test 7 times that call with the microsecond clock. It measures the host-side I2C cost only; motor current and mechanical onset cannot be measured on this bench (no current sense or scope hook).

docs.title: Test menu (i2c_test)
docs.text:
Flash with scripts/flash.sh rp2350 i2c_test; menu on UART0 at 115200. q stops a running test (any key stops the effect sweep).

Key Test Notes 1 Bus scan idle-line check, scan 0x08-0x77, PASS when 0x36 and 0x5A answer; retries at 100 kHz if a device is missing or errors occur 2 Gauge dumps version/config, then 10 s of voltage, SOC and rate; SKIP if no battery 3 Gauge under load 5 s idle, 10 s with backlight 100 % and CPU busy; backlight is turned off at the end. Shows nothing if the Pico is USB-powered: the load current must flow from the battery through the gauge 4 Haptic ID STATUS, device ID (must be 7), mode, library, control registers 5 Haptic calibrate closed loop only (SKIP in open loop): auto-calibration (motor spins about 1 s); prints the measured values, then notes the restore, and a build-flag snippet 6 Haptic sweep effects 1-123, 300 ms apart (1-10 only in run-all) 7 Click latency 20 clicks, min/avg/max microseconds 8 Haptic RTP amplitude ramp 0 to 127 to 0 over 2 s 9 Soak 60 s: gauge read every 500 ms, click every 2 s; PASS only with zero I2C errors and recoveries ("clicks only" if the gauge is absent)

docs.title: When something fails
docs.text: Symptom Meaning Scan: nothing answers No ACK at all: check SDA GP20 / SCL GP21 wiring, breakout power, and that the breakout pull-ups are present Scan: lines low before start A device is holding the bus; the test tries recovery. If it stays low, power-cycle the breakouts 0x36 missing, 0x5A fine Gauge is powered from the battery side: connect a charged LiPo (a flat one makes 0x36 vanish) 0x5A missing DRV2605L power (3.3 V), wiring or EN pin Test 4: device ID not 7 A different chip or a bad read Test 5: calibration fails or never finishes Wrong ERM/LRA setting, or the motor is not connected/seated Test 9 reports errors Look at the stats line: NACKs or timeouts point at wiring or pull-ups; try 100 kHz

docs.title: Consequences for the design
docs.text:
1. Radio: the Pico-W-style CYW43439 cannot be built at JLC. Final-board options are an ESP32-S3-WROOM host (Wi-Fi/BLE on-module, no Classic BT) or an ESP32-WROOM-32E co-processor for classic BT, both deep-stocked; the Qualcomm audio module is a hand-soldered extra either way. An RM2 module (grant-covered) is the hand-placed alternative.
  2. Audio: CS43131 is a 42-piece remnant. Given the recording requirement, ES8311/ES8388 are the manufacturable choices (ADR-0012).
  3. Displays are hand-fitted parts by design; everything else on the BOM is JLC-placeable today.
  4. Mid-mount USB-C needs the 1.0 mm (CB1.0) part verified or the board goes to 1.6 mm — which the thin shell cannot afford.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Exported from the neuPod design doc (Requirements tab, 25 Oct – 1 Nov 2026). Prices are approximate UK low-volume figures. The supplier and parts list is on the Reference page; the engineering detail is on the Design page.

docs.title: Goal and scope
docs.text:
Design a drop-in replacement logic board for the iPod Classic 6G/7G that adds Wi-Fi, Bluetooth audio, microSD storage and USB-C, while reusing the original shell, click wheel and (optionally) screen.

  • Fully reversible: original board, drive and battery can go back in.
  • No soldering to original iPod parts; board connects to the existing flex cables.
  • Fills a gap: no existing product gives a Classic Wi-Fi (Sprout targets 3G/4G/mini only; Moonlit, Boxy Pixel and iFlash add BT/USB-C/storage but keep the stock SoC).
  • Target sizes: thin shell first (the donor in hand), thick shell as the easier variant.

docs.title: Target hardware
docs.text:
Donor in hand: Apple iPod Classic 6th generation, model A1238, EMC 2173, 120 GB — the thin shell (bought on eBay, 25 Oct 2026).

Item Thin Classic (120 GB, late 160 GB) Thick Classic (80 GB, early 160 GB) Overall thickness ~10.5 mm ~13.5 mm Internal depth (approx) ~8 mm ~11 mm Stock battery ~550–650 mAh ~850 mAh Stock HDD 5 mm, 1.8" ZIF 8 mm, 1.8" ZIF Opening Spring clips, stiffer Spring clips

Why 6G/7G over 4G/5G: cheapest donors (£20–40 dead-HDD units), 320×240 colour panel, bigger wheel, and the LCD/wheel were reverse-engineered by Rockbox. 6G vs 7G makes no difference to a replacement board (same shell, screen, wheel). A thin-to-thick rear-shell swap (~£10) is a cheap way to gain battery depth.

Opening: iFixit guide iPod Classic Logic Board Replacement #572. Thin metal opening tools; release clips along both long edges; open like a book hinged at the bottom-left; disconnect battery flex (bottom) and headphone/hold flex (top, ZIF) before separating; HDD on a ZIF ribbon — flip the latch before pulling.

docs.title: Compute options
docs.text:
Current preference: RP2350B as the always-on brain (Sprout Pico approach), with a footprint reserved for a Linux module (Raspberry Pi Compute Module Zero or ESP32-P4) if streaming apps are wanted later.

Raspberry Pi's Broadcom application processors (BCM2710/2711/2712, the Zero 2 W's RP3A0 SiP) are not sold to third parties, so only their microcontrollers (RP2040/RP2350) can go on a custom PCB.

Option Cores / clock RAM Wi-Fi/BT Linux PCB layers Unit cost Notes RP2350B 2× Cortex-M33 (or RISC-V) @ 150 MHz 520 KB SRAM + QSPI PSRAM (up to 8 MB) External No 4 ~£1 48 GPIO; RP2354 variants have 2 MB flash in-package; instant-on; ~40 h battery class; PIO+DMA drives parallel LCD RP2040 2× Cortex-M0+ @ 133 MHz 264 KB External No 4 ~£0.70 Too little RAM/CPU for colour UI + codecs; avoid ESP32-S3 2× Xtensa LX7 @ 240 MHz 512 KB + 8 MB PSRAM On-chip (2.4 GHz n, BLE 5) No 4 ~£2–3 Simplest single-chip Wi-Fi/BT route; classic BT A2DP needs the older ESP32, S3 is BLE-only (LE Audio) Allwinner T113-S3 2× Cortex-A7 @ 1.2 GHz 128 MB DDR3 in-package External module Mainline 4 ~£4–5 QFN128, hand-reworkable; best fully-custom Linux route Rockchip RV1106 Cortex-A7 @ 1.2 GHz 256 MB in-package External Yes 4 ~£4–6 Luckfox Pico reference design Zero 2 W as module 4× Cortex-A53 @ 1 GHz (RP3A0) 512 MB LPDDR2 CYW43438 on-board Yes Carrier only ~£14 65×30×~1 mm; 6-layer board; soldered to a custom carrier; 0.3–0.6 W idle Compute Module Zero as Zero 2 W 512 MB On module Yes Carrier only ~£15–20 What Sprout Pi uses; check availability

Avoid any SoC needing external DDR (6–8 layers, impedance control).

docs.title: Connectivity
docs.text:
Required: 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, Bluetooth audio (A2DP to AirPods/headphones/speakers), USB-C for charging and drag-and-drop file transfer (mass storage), digital audio out over USB-C.

  • Radio for RP2350 route: Infineon CYW43439 over SPI (Pico W / Pico 2 W reference design is open, ~£2–3 + antenna) or an ESP32-C6 as radio co-processor over SPI (~£1.50, Wi-Fi 6 + BLE 5 only, easier to source). The C6 has no classic Bluetooth, so no A2DP; it only suits Wi-Fi.
  • Classic Bluetooth A2DP is needed for most headphones; confirm the chosen radio supports BR/EDR, not just BLE.
  • Antenna (requirement, 3 Nov 2026; revised 15 Nov 2026): the shell is a Faraday cage (anodised aluminium front, stainless steel back). The display glass is the only real opening, and an antenna behind the panel is shielded by the module's metal backplate, so the antenna is a slot cut in the steel back (see Slot antenna below). The radio module must have a u.FL connector (or a pad for a coax pigtail) so it can feed the slot. The earlier note of a "top plastic window of the 6G back" is superseded: the 6G back is all metal.
  • Final-board radio: not a bare CYW43439 (not assemblable at JLCPCB, outside the BTstack grant). Options: RM2 module, or an ESP32 with its own stack — see ADR-0007.
  • USB-C: 5.1 kΩ CC pulldowns for 5 V from C-to-C cables; USB 2.0 data; no PD needed at 1–2 A. The 30-pin aperture (~21 × 3 mm) takes a mid-mount USB-C receptacle with a small printed/CNC filler.
  • GPIO: 2× spare via the wired-remote connector (as Sprout) is a nice-to-have.

docs.title: Wi-Fi feature stages (4 Nov 2026)
docs.text:
Stage Feature Notes W1 Scan, WPA2/WPA3 join, DHCP, SNTP, reconnect backoff, radio-off-while-playing policy done on testbed W2 HTTP API + C# companion app (library sync, metadata, playlists) the reason Wi-Fi exists W3 Podcasts via the companion after W4 W4 OTA: image to SD, verify, A/B partitions (RP2350 bootrom TBYB), flash only with audio stopped and core 1 parked (ADR-0014) W5 "Play to…" (DLNA/UPnP AV) — neuPod as UPnP control point + media server: SSDP discovery of renderers (Sonos, AV receivers, TVs, smart speakers), SetAVTransportURI to a URL on neuPod's HTTP server, Play, transport/volume via RenderingControl; the renderer pulls the file from SD over HTTP with range requests. Wi-Fi only (not Bluetooth). Format is the renderer's: advertise MIME/DLNA profiles for FLAC/MP3/ALAC and grey out what it rejects; no on-device transcoding. Inverts the radio-off policy for the session. RAM ≈ 15–20 KB. AirPlay 2 not feasible (auth); RAOP to AirPort Express/shairport possible later; Chromecast Default Media Receiver possible later (TLS + protobuf). Open (25 Nov 2026): backlog CN-6 has the phone app drive network speakers with the device only serving files; which of the two drives them is not decided.

Existing kits for reference: Moonlit Market Classic Connect 2 (BT 5.2 aptX, Qi, haptics, USB-C charge; sync needs soldering), Boxy Pixel (BT 5.0 + USB-C charge only).

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
microSD, SDXC up to 2 TB, via SDIO (4-bit) for throughput; exFAT so the card is readable on a PC.

  • Push-push or hinged socket, accessible without opening the case is not possible on a Classic, so a reliable internal socket is enough.
  • Keep a 2 TB card on the test list: controller compatibility is where iFlash users hit trouble.
  • Library index/metadata cached in PSRAM or on-card database to keep browse fast with 100k+ tracks.
  • Card power (requirement, 3 Nov 2026): GPIO-controlled load switch on card VDD, so a wedged card can be power-cycled. SD clock from integer dividers only; multi-block reads capped at 128 blocks (Storage).

docs.title: v2 enhancement: High-Speed USB disk mode via SD bridge (parked 4 Nov 2026)
docs.text:
Context: the card will not be removed in normal use (opening a Classic is hard), and both candidate SoCs have Full-Speed USB only (~1 MB/s mass storage; 100 GB ≈ a day). Wi-Fi sync is 1–3 MB/s. For v1 the bulk path is USB-C mass storage for small loads and Wi-Fi sync for the rest; the initial load is accepted as slow.

v2: a USB 2.0 High-Speed SD bridge on the board takes the card in "disk mode" (stock-iPod behaviour): the PC sees a plain card reader at 20–35 MB/s with exFAT read/write; the MCU unmounts, shows "connected" and charges. Parts (JLC-class): Genesys GL823K bridge (QFN-24, 12 MHz crystal, ~$0.50) or GL3224 (USB 3.0); SD bus mux TS3A27518-class 6-channel analogue switch on one GPIO; USB D+/D− mux TS3USB221-class so the same USB-C serves the bridge by default or the MCU FS port (CDC console, DFU, USB audio out) on request; bridge powered from VBUS only. Costs ~60 mm² and three Extended part types; USB audio out is unavailable in disk mode. SoC alternative if USB speed ever becomes mandatory: ESP32-P4 (HS USB, 768 KB SRAM, 16–32 MB PSRAM, no radio, ~1 W class) — rejected for v1 on power and size.

docs.title: Display
docs.text:
Preferred upgrade: a 2.4"–2.8" IPS TFT (ST7789V / ILI9341, 240×320) replacing the stock panel; keep the stock panel as plan B.

Option Size / resolution Interface Cost Pros Cons Stock 6G/7G panel 2.5", 320×240 TN 8080-style parallel (init sequence in Rockbox ipod6g) £0 (reused) No mechanical change; fully reversible Dim, low contrast; must be driven exactly as Rockbox does IPS TFT, ST7789V / ILI9341 2.4" (~60 × 42 mm active) to 2.8", 240×320 SPI or 8080 parallel; RP2350 PIO+DMA £3–6 bare panel Near-OLED contrast; trivial to drive; what Zac Builds used Needs masking/bezel fit to the Classic window; new FPC routing Mono OLED (SSD1309 / SSD1322) 2.4–2.7", 128×64 or 256×64 SPI / 8080 £5–15 Retro Sprout look; very low power No album art, no colour Colour OLED ≤1.5" at 128×128; larger are MIPI phone panels SPI, or MIPI needing a bridge varies — Nothing practical at 2.5" 320×240; rule out

Requirement: measure the Classic's window aperture and the LCD bay in the mid-frame before choosing a panel part number.

Shortlisted panel: EastRising ER-TFT024IPS-3 — 2.4" IPS 240×320, ST7789V, bare glass, 50-pin 0.5 mm FPC. Active 36.72 × 48.96 mm, visual 38.72 × 50.96 mm, outline 42.72 × 59.26 × 2.3 mm (stock Classic panel ≈ 38 × 51 mm active, so ~1 mm margin each edge). 8080 8/9/16/18-bit, SPI, RGB; 500:1, 300 cd/m², 80° all round; VDD 2.8 V typ, backlight 4 WLED 70 mA. $6.35 direct; module version ER-TFTM024IPS-3 on eBay (BuyDisplay) ~$12.60 for prototyping. Datasheet, STEP model, ST7789V datasheet and ZIF drawing on the product page. Alternative: Ronbo RB024D12N19B (same glass, 12-pin SPI-only FPC).

Premium option: 2.4" AMOLED 450×600, Raydium RM690B0 (DisplayModule DM-AMOLED240-011, also Anders, TailorPixels, SWICN; ~£45–50 single, ~$25 Alibaba lots). Same 36.72 × 48.96 mm active area as the IPS panel so it fits the window identically; 311 ppi, 24-bit, 100,000:1, 60 Hz; QSPI/SPI/MIPI. Needs an AMOLED PMIC (TPS65632-class, AVDD ~4.6 V / ELVSS negative) and a QSPI write path (PIO on RP2350 at reduced frame rate, native on ESP32-S3). Burn-in and content-dependent power are the trade-offs. Ruled out: no OLED exists in the Classic's native 2.5" 4:3 landscape; memory-in-pixel, e-paper, micro-LED and phone MIPI AMOLEDs don't suit. Final board could carry both the 50-pin IPS and the AMOLED FPC footprints.

docs.title: Audio
docs.text:
Hi-fi DAC with headphone amp driving the original 3.5 mm jack via the existing headphone/hold-switch flex, plus Bluetooth A2DP and USB-C digital audio out.

  • Codec (3 Nov 2026, ADR-0012, proposed): ES8311 baseline, ES8388 alternative, PCM5102A as the DAC-only no-MCLK fallback. CS43131 dropped (≈42 pcs at LCSC). Open point: the ES8311 is mono.
  • I²S from the MCU; the board provides MCLK (256 fs from clk_gpout), but the codec must also run with its PLL from BCLK.
  • Audio isolation (requirement): audio runs on a dedicated bare-metal core with lock-free rings only (ADR-0011); any SoC candidate needs a spare core.
  • Codecs required: MP3, AAC, ALAC, FLAC, Opus (software decode on RP2350 is fine at 150 MHz).
  • Optional: small LRA for haptic click-wheel feedback (~£1, as Moonlit's kit).

Single jack, line or headphone: one 3.5 mm output from the DAC's headphone driver serves both; the codec's load/jack detection (CS43131 had this; check the ADR-0012 part) can switch a firmware "line mode" (fixed level, volume bypassed) when a high-impedance load is seen. No separate line-out socket.

Headphone jack — decision 4 Nov 2026 (ADR-0023): reuse the donor 6G headphone flex (3.5 mm TRRS jack, CTIA/Apple order Tip L, Ring 1 R, Ring 2 ground, Sleeve mic; hold switch; Mikey remote decoder at I²C 0x72). It fits the case hole by definition and gives L/R/ground, a mono mic input, and the Apple 3-button inline remote on the mic conductor (resistor ladder ≈ 0 / 240 / 620 Ω; decode via Mikey over I²C, or bias the mic line through ~2.2 kΩ and read an ADC). Plug detect from the jack switch or Mikey.

Recording: mono mic via the jack as standard. Stereo line-in on the same jack only via an analogue switch (dual SPDT, e.g. TS5A23157, one GPIO) that routes the L/R conductors to the codec ADC in a line-in mode; otherwise stereo in comes over USB-C audio. Decide with the codec.

Optical S/PDIF: parked. A mini-TOSLINK combo jack (Everlight PLT133/T10W class) has a taller, longer body than the donor jack and would mean abandoning the flex; it returns only if we make our own case. No GPIO is reserved for it.

Audio quality policy: lossless end-to-end on every wired/digital path. Decode once to a 32-bit mixer; no resampling unless the sink requires it; bit-perfect FLAC/ALAC to the DAC (CS43131: 32/384, ~130 dB DNR), to optical S/PDIF (24/96) and to USB-C UAC2. Dedicated low-noise analogue LDO and a 22.5792/24.576 MHz clock pair (or DAC PLL) for the DAC. Decode target: 24/96 FLAC on RP2350 (24/192 only on ESP32-S3-class).

Bluetooth codec Max bitrate Available on CYW43439 + BTstack Available on an external QCC module SBC / SBC-XQ 328k / ~500k Yes Yes AAC 256k 256k Encoder not free (FDK licence, heavy on M33) Yes aptX / aptX HD 352k / 576k No (Qualcomm licence) Yes LDAC 990k No (Sony licence) Some modules LC3 (LE Audio) ~345k Immature Varies

Decision pending: Bluetooth path = SBC-XQ on the CYW43439 (simplest, no extra parts) or an external Qualcomm QCC3008/3040/5125 transmitter module on I²S with UART control (aptX HD/AAC/LDAC, what the commercial iPod BT kits use). Wi-Fi/BT coexistence and the metal shell limit link quality either way.

Recording (new requirement, 31 Oct 2026): the board shall record audio to microSD. Sources, in priority order: (1) mono mic on a 4-pole headset plugged into the 3.5 mm jack; (2) Bluetooth headset mic (HFP, voice quality only); (3) optional on-board MEMS mic for voice notes; (4) USB-C audio in. Target formats: WAV 48 kHz/16-bit for the jack and MEMS paths; whatever the BT profile delivers for HFP. The codec/DAC chosen must therefore include an ADC input (CS43131 is DAC-only — either add a small ADC such as a PCM1808/ES8311/WM8960-class codec, or move to a combined codec part). Keep the ADC analogue front end on its own clean LDO, away from the switcher, same as the DAC.

3.5 mm jack = 4-pole TRRS, CTIA pinout (tip L, ring 1 R, ring 2 GND, sleeve mic). Requirements:

  • Mic bias ~2.0–2.7 V via ~2.2 kΩ, switchable off in firmware.
  • Inline-button decode: headsets short the mic line through resistors (play/pause ≈ 0 Ω, vol+ ≈ 240 Ω, vol− ≈ 600 Ω); read with an ADC channel on the mic line and map to click-wheel actions.
  • Jack insert detect (switched contact on the socket or codec jack-detect) to route headphone/line/optical and to disable mic bias when a 3-pole TRS plug is present (its sleeve is ground).
  • Design for CTIA only; OMTP (mic/GND swapped) headsets are not supported.
  • The optical-combo socket option above must still be 4-pole if chosen; check availability (optical + TRRS combos are rarer than optical + TRS).

Bluetooth profiles required: A2DP source for stereo playback — neuPod sends audio to the headphones/speaker, which are the A2DP sink (SBC/AAC minimum; aptX/LDAC per the transmitter decision above). AVRCP (neuPod as target, the headset as controller) for play/pause/next/previous from the headset buttons, plus absolute volume so the headset's volume and neuPod's are one control. HFP in the Audio Gateway role for the headset mic — note it drops both directions to 8/16 kHz mono (CVSD/mSBC), so BT recording is voice-note quality only. LE Audio / LC3 (stereo, bidirectional, good quality) is a nice-to-have: pick a radio whose stack can do LE Audio so it can be enabled later. Reference headset for testing: Stuart's AirPods Pro 3 (model A3063/A3064, 2025, Apple H2) — A2DP + AAC for playback, HFP for mic; LE Audio only via Apple's own path, so not usable for LC3 testing.

docs.title: Power and battery
docs.text:
Target: 2,000+ mAh in the thin shell, 3,000 mAh in the thick shell; 40 h Bluetooth playback is the benchmark (Sprout's figure with 2,500 mAh).

Shell Cell thickness available Candidate cells Capacity Thin (donor) ~4 mm once HDD + original board are gone (~1 mm board) 405080, 4055100-class pouch ~2,000–2,500 mAh Thick ~6–7 mm 605070 / 605080, 7 mm variants ~3,000–3,500 mAh Stock reference thin 550–650 mAh, thick 850 mAh; aftermarket thin ~1,000–1,200 mAh, thick 3,000 mAh (with stock board + iFlash)
  • Cells with built-in PCM (OV/UV/OC protection); thermistor input on the board.
  • Charger (3 Nov 2026): BQ25895 (I²C 0x6A, INT pin, full status registers, OTG, power-path). Firmware models its state machine in hal_charger.h; the testbed (Micro-Lipo MCP73831, no STAT pin) is a second implementation: VBUS present (cyw43 WL_GPIO2) AND MAX17048 CRATE > 0 = charging; VBUS AND CRATE ≈ 0 AND SOC ≥ 98 % = full.
  • Fuel gauge for real percentage in the UI: BQ27441 or MAX17048.
  • Rails: 3.3 V for MCU/radio/SD, clean analogue rail for the DAC, LCD backlight boost.
  • Power states: instant-on from sleep (RP2350 dormant mode), deep sleep when hold is on, hard off.

Power budget by state (estimates, to be measured on the bench):

Block Standby Playing, screen off, BT RP2350 core ~1 mA sleep / 0.2 mA dormant 25–40 mA ESP32-S3 core + octal PSRAM ~10 µA deep sleep / ~2 mA light 60–100 mA CYW43439 BT A2DP <1 mA 30–50 mA QCC3008-class BT module ~1 mA 20–35 mA microSD <0.2 mA ~10 mA average (bursts to 60) CS43131 DAC + HP amp off 10–25 mA 2.4" IPS + backlight off 100–150 mA when on 2.4" AMOLED off 40–200 mA when on, content dependent Regulators, gauge, misc ~1 mA ~5 mA

Totals playing to BT, screen off: architecture A (RP2350 + CYW43439) ~80–110 mA → 23–30 h on 2,500 mAh; architecture B (ESP32-S3 + QCC) ~110–160 mA → 16–22 h. Idle policy (ADR-0021): after Sleep after (Never, 10, 30 default, 60 min) of nothing happening, off external power, the player suspends (Bluetooth controller off, settings and resume position written out first); a day asleep powers it off, and so does a battery at or below 3 % for 30 s; a paused player counts as idle, a playing one does not. Standby target <0.5 mA: load switches on SD, DAC and radio rails; wake from hold switch or wheel. Backlight dims to ~10% after the idle time (default 30 s) and goes fully off 3 min after that (Settings > Display, both adjustable; ADR-0020; this replaces the earlier "off within ~15 s": the totals above assume the screen off, so a listening session pays the 3.5 minutes of display once, after each press); Wi-Fi off during playback; core clock scaled to the minimum that keeps the audio buffer full.

docs.title: Reused parts and mechanical
docs.text:
Reuse the shell, mid-frame, click wheel and its FPC, headphone/hold-switch flex, and (plan B) the LCD. Everything connects via the original ribbons into FPC/ZIF connectors on the new board.

Known internal geometry (open sources; everything else comes from the donor scan): envelope 103.5 × 61.8 × 10.5 mm thin / 13.5 mm thick (everymac). Stack front→back: front plate + glass; click wheel and LCD on a steel backing plate; metal mid-frame; logic board (full footprint, ~95 × 55 × 1.0 mm, two screws to the frame, connectors on its edges and back face); battery pouch on the board; 1.8" ZIF HDD in foam bumpers — Toshiba MK8022GAA/MK1231GAL/MK1634GAL, 54 × 71 × 5 mm thin or 8 mm thick; stainless back shell (iFixit teardown). Usable depth for our board + cell: ~6 mm thin, ~9 mm thick. Board silicon and revisions (A1238 120 GB = Rev A, 2008): S5L8702, K4X51163PE SDRAM, SST25VF080B flash, PCF50635 PMU, CS42L55 codec, LTC4066 charger (freemyipod). Not published anywhere: board/mid-frame drawings, 6G connector pitches, battery outline, screw positions.

From the donor teardown (5 Nov 2026, Teardown): the mid-frame is a ribbed casting — the board (Apple 820-2437) is screwed behind it and the ribs split the board area into ~six pockets (~25 × 18 mm); tall parts only fit in the pockets, ~1 mm under the ribs. The battery is in the back shell, not on the board, so the board side has the frame plus the whole HDD cavity — more depth than the 6 mm estimate — and a thicker cell can go in the shell. Jack + hold switch are one flex in the shell's top-left corner. The logic board measures 55 × 45 mm (47 mm over the middle tabs), 0.4 mm thick — lower half of the frame under the wheel, nothing behind the LCD — so usable PCB area is ~25 cm², not the 95 × 55 mm in the open-source notes. The curved 15 mm-wide tab at the top exists only to carry the top button's footprint. The five wheel buttons are 6 × 6 mm tact switches on the logic board's wheel-facing side (centre + four at ≈ 13.5 mm radius, two wheel-locating holes, a clear ≈ 37 mm circle) — the new board must reproduce them. Connectors on the board: LCD ZIF (wide), wheel FPC (flex 631-0457, 13 positions at 0.3 mm, confirmed by ruler; likely carries the five switch lines to the wheel PSoC), jack/hold flex, battery, HDD ZIF, 30-pin dock. Outline, screw holes, pitches and rib heights are the next measurements. Volumes: HDD cavity 70 × 55 × 7 mm (incl. bumpers) over the ribs → room for a 505060/605060 LiPo (2,500–3,000 mAh) on the board side; donor battery pocket 45 × 20 × 5 mm in the shell freed for a haptic actuator. The battery is replaced, so its connector is our choice (2-pin PH/MX1.25 or 3-pin with thermistor, decided with the charger).

  • Board outline: match the original logic board's outline and the mid-frame screw holes (two Phillips screws); design to the mid-frame, not the shell. Original board ~1.6 mm; target 1.0–1.2 mm.
  • Connectors to provide: click wheel FPC, LCD FPC (stock pinout or new panel), headphone/hold flex, battery (3-pin, thermistor), microSD socket, USB-C mid-mount.
  • Click wheel: keep; serial protocol documented in Rockbox; new wheels available from Elite Obsolete.
  • Port aperture: 30-pin opening ~21 × 3 mm; USB-C with printed/CNC filler. Keep the port centred.
  • Antenna: slot in the steel back near the top edge; keep-out behind it. See Slot antenna.
  • Thermal/EMI: metal shell; no thermal issue at RP2350 power levels.
  • Reversibility: no adhesive on original parts; foam spacers where the HDD was.
  • Cosmetic parts if needed: Elite Obsolete (shells, wheels, faceplates), Moonlit Market, iFlash (shells, screws, tools).

docs.title: Slot antenna
docs.text:
Working design for the 2.4 GHz antenna (Wi-Fi and Bluetooth share it). Recorded 15 Nov 2026; nothing here has been cut or measured yet.

  • Where: a closed slot in the stainless back, parallel to and about 4–6 mm in from the top edge (the hold switch and headphone jack end). That end is clear of the hand that holds the bottom and of the wheel. Centre it across the 61.8 mm width.
  • Size: about 1.5 mm wide. Length is λ/2 at 2.44 GHz: 61 mm in air, shortened by the filler. With an epoxy or polycarbonate fill (εr ≈ 3, εeff ≈ 2) expect ~43–50 mm. Cut it short first and lengthen it while tuning. The slot needs unbroken metal around it, at least ~5 mm on every side, with no seams or screw holes in that margin.
  • Fallback if a closed slot won't fit or tune: an open-ended λ/4 slot, ~25–30 mm long, running in from the edge. It cuts the rim, so it's structurally and cosmetically worse.
  • Feed: a small FR4 or FPC feed board bonded inside the back over the slot. A 50 Ω microstrip crosses the slot about 10–20 % of its length from one end (the slot centre is roughly 500 Ω, the ends are a short), finishing in an open λg/4 stub past the slot. A U.FL connector on the board carries a pigtail to the radio. This avoids soldering to stainless, and moving the crossing point is the main matching adjustment. The feed board's ground must bond to the back on both sides of the slot (conductive adhesive tape or spring fingers).
  • Back grounding: the back must be tied to system ground at several points (spring contacts to the board or mid-frame). If it floats, the slot's resonance moves around.
  • Keep-out: keep at least 3 mm of air or foam behind the slot and feed board, with no battery pouch, PCB copper or flex over it. The battery is a metal laminate and detunes the slot badly. On the thin back (~6 mm usable depth) this sets where the cell can sit. That's one more reason for the thick back.
  • Fill and finish: fill flush with black epoxy or a press-fit polycarbonate strip, and tune with the fill in place because the filler shifts the resonance. Cut it by wire EDM (cleanest on the curved shell) or fibre laser. Deburr, and don't leave a burr bridging the gap.
  • Pass criteria: S11 below −10 dB across 2.400–2.4835 GHz on a NanoVNA, measured with the back assembled, the battery fitted, and a hand on the bottom half. Then compare received RSSI against a bare dev board using the ESP32 probe's Wi-Fi scan, which prints per-network RSSI.
  • Qi option: a plastic or glass back for Qi charging makes the slot unnecessary. The antenna then sits under the plastic, with the same keep-out from the coil and cell.
  • Option to test: PCB-trace antenna under or around the wheel. The click wheel and its centre button are plastic, and the gap between the wheel's rim and the aluminium front plate is a natural annular slot. Test a printed antenna on our board in that region: a meandered inverted-F (TI DN007 / AN043 style) or a trace that follows part of the wheel's outline. It costs nothing in BOM and needs no machining of the shell. Unknowns to settle on the bench:
  • The wheel flex has its own copper (16 sense segments plus ground) and sits directly over the board. A trace under the wheel is probably shadowed and detuned, so the rim gap is the likelier spot.
  • Whether the steel backing plate and the metal mid-frame leave any clear path from the board's edge to the rim gap.
  • Coupling into the wheel's capacitive sensing: check that radio TX bursts don't cause false touches or position jitter. Also check the reverse, that the wheel's ~53 kHz scan doesn't desense the receiver.
  • Detuning by the thumb, which rests right on top of it.
  • Test method: a sacrificial test PCB in the board outline with two or three trace variants (and a u.FL on each for comparison), measured with a NanoVNA inside the closed shell, then an RSSI comparison against the slot using the ESP32 probe's scan. If it passes, it may replace the slot. If not, the slot stays the plan.

Click wheel sub-board (how it works): a capacitive ring of ~16 copper segments under the plastic plus five dome switches, scanned by a microcontroller on the flex itself (Cypress PSoC on the 5G; same family on the 6G). The PSoC interpolates finger position to 96 steps per revolution and streams 32-bit frames on its own ~53 kHz clock while touched; the host only listens (one init packet). It has its own 3.0 V LDO fed from the system rail. All the touch logic therefore stays in the wheel — our board needs 4 lines + power and a frame decoder (design doc §4.1).

Click feedback — direction set 3 Nov 2026: the final board carries both a piezo footprint (stock feel) and an LRA footprint (LD0832AA, stocked); A/B on the testbed before freezing. The Click feedback setting becomes piezo / haptic / off. Background: The stock iPod has no haptic: the click is a piezo buzzer on the logic board driven as a tone (Rockbox piezo-6g.c). Options: (a) piezo only — authentic, ~£0.50, one GPIO/PWM; (b) LRA or ERM haptic via DRV2605L on I²C — the Moonlit Classic Connect feel, ~£5, needs board area near the wheel; (c) both, selectable in settings. Board footprints for both are cheap; the decision is about mid-frame space and whether the original feel matters.

docs.title: Firmware
docs.text:
Click-wheel-driven UI recreating the Classic experience (menus, Cover Flow, podcasts, search), audio pipeline with software codecs, BT/Wi-Fi stacks, USB mass storage. This is the largest cost in the project — more than the hardware.

  • Starting points: Rockbox ipod6g target (LCD init, click wheel protocol, headphone detect); Sprout's open-source firmware (MPL-2.0) once published at github.com/seanpod/sprout; sPot (Guy Dupont) for a Pi/Spotify UI.
  • Wi-Fi use cases: podcast download, library sync from a NAS/PC, firmware OTA. Streaming (Spotify/Apple Music) needs a Linux module.
  • Host side: the iPod must mount as a plain USB drive — no iTunes dependency.
  • Keep the stock-panel driver and a new-panel driver behind one display abstraction so either screen works.
  • RAM budget: every feature ADR states its RAM cost (the Pico 2 W's 520 KB is no longer a limit since 12 Nov 2026: the product target is the RP2350B with PSRAM, ADR-0001 amendment). The final board has 8 MB PSRAM (APS6404L, QSPI CS1, ADR-0013); artwork, HTTP and AAC are PSRAM-only.
  • Flash and OTA: final board 16 MB W25Q128; bootrom A/B partitions with TBYB (ADR-0014).
  • Secrets: RP2350 random 256-bit key in OTP at provisioning, chip-ID HKDF as the pre-provisioning fallback, no secure element; ESP32 route: eFuse key + flash encryption. Secure boot decided later (Wi-Fi).
  • Clock: ADR-0015.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
Manufacturability rule (2 Nov 2026): every part on the final BOM must be stocked at LCSC and placeable by JLCPCB (Basic/Preferred preferred, Extended accepted with its feeder fee) or be explicitly flagged as hand-placed (AMOLED panel, IPS panel, Bluetooth audio module, optical jack if it ever returns). Check stock in the JLC BOM tool at order time; the 2 Nov survey is in Reference. Five 4-layer 100 × 60 mm boards assembled come to ≈ £360 (Economic, single-side) to £430 (Standard) landed, feeder fees dominating.

About £35–55 in parts per board (RP2350 route ~£25–40), before the donor iPod and battery; budget £300–600 for two or three prototype spins including assembly. Figures are approximate, low-volume UK pricing, October 2026.

Item Estimate Compute: RP2350B / ESP32-S3 / T113 £1–5 Compute: Zero 2 W or CM Zero (module route) £14–20 DAC + headphone amp (CS43131 / ES9018K2M) £5–8 Charger, fuel gauge, regulators £4–6 Wi-Fi/BT (CYW43439 or ESP32-C6, if not on-chip) £2–5 microSD socket, USB-C, FPC/ZIF connectors £3–4 Passives, crystals, ESD, antenna £3–5 PCB, 4-layer, JLCPCB, 5 pcs £20–40 per batch (6-layer ~double) Assembly £5–15 per board, or hand-build Battery 2,000–3,000 mAh £10–15 Donor Classic £25–40 (already bought) Replacement IPS panel (optional) £3–6 Thick rear shell (optional) ~£10

docs.title: Waveshare RP2350-Touch-AMOLED-2.41 (dev board)
docs.text:
The product runtime (neupod) also builds for this board, as a second board of the RP2350 platform (-DNEUPOD_BOARD=amoled241; the default, pico2w, is unchanged). It is a dev board: it has an RP2350B with PSRAM and a touch AMOLED, which is the shape of the final board's compute and display, but no radio, no audio and no click wheel.

scripts/build.sh rp2350-amoled241                                 # -> build/rp2350-amoled241/platforms/rp2350/neupod.uf2
picotool load -f -x build/rp2350-amoled241/platforms/rp2350/neupod.uf2   # a running image reboots into BOOTSEL by itself

(scripts/build.sh rp2350-amoled241 is cmake -S . -B build/rp2350-amoled241 -G Ninja -DNEUPOD_PLATFORM=rp2350 -DNEUPOD_BOARD=amoled241. NEUPOD_BOARD has to be chosen when the build directory is created, because it selects the SDK's board header: use a separate build directory per board.)

The console is the USB serial port (CDC; it shows up as /dev/serial/by-id/usb-Raspberry_Pi_Pico_*): the board's UART0 pins are not brought out. UART0 stays enabled as well (the panic path writes to it).

On a Linux desktop ModemManager probes a new serial port for a minute or so, so a terminal may not be able to open it at once, and the boot lines printed in the meantime are lost; open the port as soon as it opens and press the reset button (or reflash) to see them again. The runtime keeps printing a heartbeat and the audio, UI and Wi-Fi statistics every 10 s.

docs.title: What is different from the Pico 2 W build
docs.text:
Part Pico 2 W amoled241 Board header SDK pico2_w platforms/rp2350/boards/amoled241/waveshare_rp2350_touch_amoled_2.41.h (RP2350B, 16 MB flash) Display ST7789 320x240, SPI1 + DMA RM690B0 AMOLED, 450x600 native, used as 600x450 landscape; QSPI by one PIO state machine + DMA (hal_display_rm690b0.c, rm690b0_qspi.pio) Touch none FT6336 on I2C1 (hal_touch.h, hal_touch_ft6336.c) Input click wheel (PIO) no wheel (hal_input_init reports "no receiver"; the boot check marks the wheel unavailable); the Power button (GPIO24) is the one key Radio CYW43439 Wi-Fi + Bluetooth, lwIP, BTstack none: hal_radio_none.c (Wi-Fi "not present", Bluetooth cannot start; the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth screens show "unavailable") Audio I2S DAC (Audio Pack) none: the null sink microSD SDIO 4-bit SPI0 (SCK 18, MOSI 19, MISO 20, CS 23), the same carlk3 library in SPI mode (hal_storage_spi.c, hw_config.c) Fuel gauge, haptics MAX17048, DRV2605L on I2C0 none (the I2C1 bus only answers the addresses of the parts the board has, so those boot checks report "absent" without touching the touch controller) Power USB battery with a soft latch: GPIO25 (BAT_Control) is driven high at the start of hal_system_init, low = off Status LED on the CYW43 chip none Clock 125 MHz 125 MHz (QSPI SCLK = 62.5 MHz)

Not built for this board: the display_test, i2c_test and storage_test executables (Pico 2 W bench tools).

docs.title: Pins
docs.text: Function GPIO AMOLED CS / CLK / D0..D3 / RST / TE / PWR_EN 9 / 10 / 11..14 / 15 / 16 (unused) / 17 Touch SDA / SCL / INT / RST 6 / 7 / 4 (unused: polled) / 5 microSD SCK / MOSI / MISO / CS 18 / 19 / 20 / 23 Power key (KEY_BAT, active low) / BAT_Control 24 / 25 Battery ADC (x3 divider) 40 (not read: no battery reading in the UI yet) PSRAM (QMI CS1) 47 (not used by the firmware yet)

docs.title: Display notes
docs.text:
• Orientation. The panel's own MADCTL (0x36) is 0xA0 (MY|MV) by default: the controller addresses itself as landscape, with a page (row) offset of 16 (the 450 visible columns sit 16 from one end of the controller's 480-column memory and 14 from the other; the offset has to be the one on the side the mirror bit makes "first", else a 2 px band of unused memory shows on an edge). -DNEUPOD_AMOLED_LANDSCAPE=3 turns the picture by 180 degrees (MADCTL 0x60, offset 14) and the touch mapping with it, so the pair stays consistent. On the owner's bench, MADCTL 0x60 with the touch mapping below (landscape x = raw y, y = 449 - raw x) was 180 degrees apart; the default is therefore the rotated display with that touch mapping. The offsets come from other RM690B0 drivers; whether a band shows on an edge has not been checked by eye by me.
  • Even windows. The controller addresses whole pixel pairs: hal_display_set_window() returns HAL_EINVAL for an odd x, y, width or height. The UI rounds its flush areas outwards (LVGL rounder).
  • Brightness is the panel's own register (0x51): hal_display_backlight() 0..255. hal_display_sleep() sends DISPOFF + SLPIN.
  • The build selects the UI profile 600x450 automatically.

docs.title: Touch notes
docs.text: hal_touch_read() returns the first contact in the display's landscape coordinates (x 0..599, y 0..449). The raw controller values are portrait (x 0..449, y 0..599): landscape x = raw y, landscape y = 449 - raw x. -DNEUPOD_AMOLED_TOUCH_LOG=ON logs every press, a move every 200 ms and the release with raw and mapped values (off by default: a USB terminal that is attached but not reading can block the input task). The chip ID line is always logged at init. The input task initialises the controller (it logs its chip, vendor and firmware IDs) and reads the points under the I2C mutex.

docs.title: Storage notes
docs.text: SDHC and SDXC cards only (the library's SPI mode refuses standard-capacity cards). The SPI clock is 20.8 MHz (125 MHz / 6). There is no SD Status register (so no speed class or allocation unit in the card info), no CMD6 and no bus-clock change in this mode; those HAL calls answer "unsupported". The write guard, mounting, formatting and the music library work as on the Pico 2 W.

docs.title: Power notes
docs.text: The Power key held for 10 s shows the "shutting down" countdown (hal_system_can_poweroff() is true); at the end the runtime lets the card finish its writes and drops BAT_Control. On battery the board then switches off when the key is released. On USB power it cannot: the request is refused and the latch is closed again. After dropping the latch the HAL waits for the key to be released (at most 3 s, in the UI task) and then 0.5 s more; still running means USB power. No VBUS or charger-status line is read (the schematic was not checked for one). The Power key is read as level; the press that switched the board on is not counted.

docs.title: What is not done
docs.text:
• PSRAM (8 MB on QMI CS1) is not initialised by the firmware; the driver of the bring-up probe (testbed/amoled241/bringup/src/psram.c) is the starting point.
  • No battery voltage (GPIO40 through the x3 divider) and no RTC / IMU.
  • Display and touch orientation, and brightness, have been checked through the registers and the console only.

docs.title: Runtime: RTOS, audio core and boot
docs.text: The neupod executable (RP2350 and host) is this runtime. Decisions: ADR-0011 (single-core FreeRTOS on core 0, bare-metal audio core on core 1; amends ADR-0009) and ADR-0010 (LVGL). The RTOS task table lives in app/include/runtime_config.h; this page explains it.

docs.title: Cores
docs.text: Core Runs Rules 0 FreeRTOS (single-core kernel): UI, input, storage, monitor, CYW43 worker, boot checks normal RTOS code 1 the bare-metal audio core: a main loop (commands + "decoder": silence, test signals, WAV conversion) and the sink's block interrupt (the I2S DMA interrupt); no kernel the core-1 rules below

docs.title: Core-1 rules
docs.text: Core 1 code (app/audio/audio_core.c, audio_shared.c, audio_dsp.c, spsc_ring.c, the headers they use, and platforms/rp2350/hal/hal_audio.c / hal_audio_null.c) must not use: FreeRTOS or os.h; stdio (printf); malloc; any SDK primitive the FreeRTOS interop reroutes to the kernel (mutex, semaphore, queue, critical section, sleep_*, busy_wait_*); hal_delay_ms. It talks to core 0 only through lock-free rings and a seqlock. Hardware registers, the 1 MHz timer reads (time_us_64, hal_micros) and the SDK's spin-lock-only alarm API are fine. The ctest audio_core_rules (cmake/check_core1_rules.cmake) fails the build on forbidden tokens in those files.

docs.title: Hot path in RAM
docs.text: on_block, the ring functions, the alarm interrupt (block_isr, driven straight from the timer registers, no SDK alarm code and no spin lock shared with core 0) and hal_micros run from RAM (NEUPOD_RAM_FUNC, __not_in_flash_func) so the audio core does not contend with the UI for the XIP flash cache. memcpy and memset (newlib, flash) are still used by the ring. Core 1's stack is painted at start and its high-water mark is printed in the audio line (core1_stack_free=).

docs.title: Core 0 / core 1 communication
docs.text:
From to Mechanism core 0 to 1: commands ring of audio_cmd_t (open, close, statistics window, volume, tone, stream start, stream next, pause, stop); several core-0 tasks send, so audio_ctl.c serialises them with a mutex core 0 to 1: stream data byte ring, 32 KB, fed by the storage task while a file plays: raw WAV bytes, compressed FLAC / MP3 bytes, or length-prefixed ALAC packets core 0 to 1: stream slots two slots (seq & 1) with the stream description and its byte length (published once its last byte is in the ring), plus g_audio_next_valid (the announced successor, cleared to cancel); see Audio core 1 to 0: seek request request counter plus byte offset, acknowledged by core 0, flush acknowledged by core 1 (stream_io.h) core 1 to 0: handshake counters written only by core 1: streams set up / ended with nothing following (core 0 must not write data for a new stream before the first moves), the sequence number of the open decoder, and gapless handoffs completed (written by the block interrupt) core 1 to 0: events two rings (one per producer: the block interrupt, the main loop): stream opened/closed, underrun (at most ~1/s), end of track, command error core 1 to 0: statistics seqlock-published audio_stats_t, written only by the block interrupt inside core 1: decoder to sink PCM ring, 4096 stereo int32 frames (16 blocks, 93 ms at 44.1 kHz)

Every ring has exactly one producer and one consumer (spsc_ring.h: acquire/release loads and stores only, no read-modify-write, so it is safe across the two cores).

docs.title: How audio timing works
docs.text: With NEUPOD_AUDIO_SINK=null (or on the host) the sink arms a 1 MHz hardware alarm from core 1; its interrupt fires every 256 frames (5.8 ms at 44.1 kHz) on absolute deadlines (no drift) and runs on_block, which reads one block from the PCM ring (silence and an underrun if the decoder starved it), applies the volume ramp, hands it to the sink and updates the statistics and the amp mute line. The interrupt preempts the decoder (-DNEUPOD_DECODER_LOAD_PCT=25 makes it busy-spend 25 % of a block period per block, as the old stub did, to prove it), so block timing does not depend on decoder time. The main loop sleeps with WFI when idle. Nothing on core 0 can delay it: no shared lock, no kernel, no shared interrupt. The I2S sink (default on the RP2350, see Audio) uses the same structure with the DMA block-complete interrupt (DMA_IRQ_1, core 1) instead of the alarm.

docs.title: RTOS tasks (core 0)
docs.text:
Priority 7 is the highest; the kernel idle task is 0.
